data.title: Pobedim – a Slavic lowland hillfort in the Dudváh floodplain
data.excerpt: Pobedim in the floodplain of the Dudváh is one of the oldest hillforts of the Slavs north of the Danube: a lowland fortified settlement with an acropolis and an outer bailey, defended by a timber-and-earth rampart with a stone facing and a palisade. The excavation by Darina Bialeková reconstructed its construction down to the timber used, put the cost of the defences at some 49,300 work shifts for 812 running metres, and showed that the hillfort burnt down before Great Moravia arose.
data.metaTitle: Pobedim – a Slavic lowland hillfort on the Dudváh
data.metaDescription: A lowland Slavic hillfort in the Dudváh floodplain, one of the oldest north of the Danube. The excavation by Darina Bialeková reconstructed its rampart.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: South-west of the present-day village of Pobedim, in the floodplain of the Dudváh and the Dubová; a lowland fortified settlement using the water regime as protection (as at Mikulčice, Pohansko near Břeclav, Majcichov)

keyFacts.label: Area
keyFacts.value: Hradištia 4.1 ha, Podhradištia 3.9 ha — not large in total, yet one of the oldest hillforts of the Slavs north of the Danube

keyFacts.label: Rampart construction (Hradištia)
keyFacts.value: Chambered; chambers c. 4 × 4 m, total width with the stone wall 5.5 m, height without the palisade 2.4 m; the wall of quarried stone 1.5 m thick at the base

keyFacts.label: Rampart construction (Podhradištia)
keyFacts.value: Simpler; chambers c. 3 × 3 m with wattled walls, total width 4.5 m, height 2.3 m

keyFacts.label: Ditch
keyFacts.value: Depth 2.05 m, width at the upper edge 5.70 m, pointed profile

keyFacts.label: Material consumption
keyFacts.value: Building the defences at Hradištia (812 running metres) required some 49,300 work shifts — with 190 people and a ten-hour day, about 260 days of work

keyFacts.label: Defence
keyFacts.value: An estimated 260 defenders (one for every 5 m of rampart), drawn also from 8 surrounding settlements

children.text: Pobedim is a well-known archaeological site. Its most important discovery was the uncovering of a Slavic hillfort from the period of Pribina's principality. The archaeological excavation at the locality known as Hradištia was led by PhDr. Darina Bialeková CSc., who became an honorary citizen of the village.

The earliest occupation of Pobedim dates from the Neolithic and the Eneolithic, when the first farmers settled in the cadastral area of the village. The occupation is attested by pottery sherds and parts of stone tools at the locality known as Hradištia. Further evidence of occupation was uncovered here during the excavation, this time from the Early Bronze Age. Of the Bronze Age, however, the most important is the occupation of the Late and Final Bronze Age. During ten years of excavation a settlement belonging to the people of the Lusatian culture was investigated. Several settlement features were uncovered, as well as a cult place of worshippers of the sun god. Among the finds, moulds for casting bronze objects, pottery, worked bone and above all a rich collection of bronze objects (pins, sickles, small knives, arrowheads, jewellery and others) deserve attention. From the mass of pottery fragments it was possible to reconstruct vessels of various types, and small animal figurines were not lacking either. The Final Bronze Age settlement was an important production, trade and cult centre in the middle Váh region.

blocks.caption: The hillfort clearly visible on the Second Military Survey
blocks.alt: The hillfort clearly visible on the Second Military Survey

children.text: A Roman figurine of Silenus

The occupation of Pobedim was also significant in the period when the territory of present-day Slovakia lay next to the Roman Empire. At the locality known as Dolné pole a settlement with notable finds from the Roman period was investigated. Settlement features were uncovered and pottery vessels found, and particularly valuable are the fragments of Roman pottery, the so-called terra sigillata. Roman coins made the dating of the finds easier. These appeared both at the site of Dolné pole and at the locality known as Horné pole. An important and frequently published find from the Roman period is a bronze head of Silenus inlaid with silver. Features of a production character were found and documented during the construction of the motorway between Piešťany and Horná Streda. The continuity of occupation at Pobedim can be traced into the Migration Period as well.

blocks.alt: The hillfort on an orthophoto map from the 1950s, before its destruction

children.text: The first Slavs appeared in the cadastral area of the village in the 6th century, when early Slavic settlements lay at the localities known as Dolné pole and Horné pole. From there, in the 8th century, the occupation moved from the catchment of the Dudváh and the Dubová. The most intensive Slavic occupation, however, was at the end of the 8th and the beginning of the 9th century. Several localities in the cadastral area of the village were inhabited at that time, but the most important was the locality known as Zapupovec, where almost 30 features were investigated, two of them wells. On the evidence of the finds, the inhabitants of the settlement practised smithing. This is attested by finds of tuyères, iron slag and unfinished products. Besides these finds, the discovery of a wooden ladle in well 1 and finds of two decorative sheet-metal mounts are worthy of attention.
The defences of the Slavic hillfort

Without doubt the most important Slavic archaeological site was the fortified centre, which had its own acropolis and an outer bailey. It extended over the localities known as Hradištia and Podhradištia. The hillfort is one of the oldest hillforts of the Slavs north of the Danube. It was defended by a rampart built using a chamber system. On the outer side, a stone wall protected the earthen rampart reinforced with timber, and on the inner side the rampart was supported by inclined braces. A timber palisade was set into the crown of the rampart. Watchtowers stood at certain points along the rampart. A magnate resided in the fortified centre with his retinue and his servants. Workshops lay close to the rampart, while the centre of the hillfort was a place where the inhabitants of the surrounding settlements could gather in times of danger. The Pobedim hillfort was also a centre of trade in the Váh basin. This statement is supported by archaeological finds, and above all by finds of axe-shaped currency bars — iron bars shaped like elongated axes, at that time a semi-finished product and a primitive form of currency.

children.text: VÝSKUM A REKONŠTRUKCIA FORTIFIKÁCIE NA SLOVANSKOM HRADISKU V POBEDIME (Excavation and reconstruction of the fortification at the Slavic hillfort in Pobedim)

The Pobedim hillfort can be characterised as one of the few typical lowland fortified settlements in the territory of present-day Slovakia that used the natural water regime as protection — e.g. Mikulčice, Pohansko near Břeclav, Majcichov (Chropovský 1964, pp. 15, 17) and others. The earliest mentions of the ramparts of the original Slavic fortification date from the end of the 19th century. P. Jedlicska (1891) states that the rampart on the northern side of Hradištia was the boundary between the cadastral areas of Pobedim and Očkov. In the description of the village of Pobedim in the work Magyarország vármegyéi és városai — Nyitravármegye (The counties and towns of Hungary — Nyitra County), remains of a wall are mentioned at a place called Hradište, where „there may have been some kind of fortification" (Sziklay — Borovszky 1898, p. 166).

The size and internal division of the hillfort were determined by historical and social factors, but the shape of the hillfort was largely adapted to the configuration of the terrain. The Pobedim hillfort is situated south-west of the present-day village, in the floodplain of the Dudváh and the Dubová, and takes in the whole of the locality known as Hradištia and almost half of the locality known as Podhradištia. The usable area of the first part (Hradištia) is 4.1 ha, the usable area of the second part (Podhradištia) 3.9 ha. It is essentially not a large hillfort. Its earlier name was Hradište, as documented by the cadastral map of 1900. The archaeological excavation of the hillfort's fortification, especially at the south-western bend of the rampart, produced convincing evidence that Hradištia was fortified first and the Podhradištia enclosure soon afterwards. It is hard to say, however, whether Hradištia then retained a position of priority, at most the function of an acropolis, because the finds from both parts of the hillfort are dated to the same period, are of equal informative value, and similar tendencies can be observed in the distribution of the features as well (the inclination of the features towards the vicinity of the rampart). In neither part of the hillfort were traces of more significant secular or sacred architecture found.

blocks.caption: Axe-shaped currency bars from Pobedim – the currency of the Slavs
blocks.alt: Axe-shaped currency bars from Pobedim – the currency of the Slavs

children.text: At the time the excavation began, the marshy ground of the former cadastral area of Očkov extended on the northern and western sides of the hillfort; it was drained only after 1959. The character of the surrounding terrain evidently had a decisive importance in the choice of the place for building this fortified centre. Taking into account the former course of the Dudváh, which probably meandered close to the hillfort, it has to be assumed that the area between the stream and the hillfort was always so marshy that it became the natural protection of the hillfort along its entire northern, western and south-western side and partly also along its southern side.

Alongside the excavation of the fortification, the settlement and production features were also investigated; at the hillfort these were concentrated above all near the defences. The bulk of all the finds, including the hoards of axe-shaped currency bars, was concentrated there as well.
The construction of the rampart at Hradištia.

blocks.caption: The construction of the rampart – shell construction with chamber reinforcement
blocks.alt: The construction of the rampart – shell construction with chamber reinforcement

children.text: In the part called Hradištia it was established that the rampart was constructed of chambers measuring c. 4 × 4 m. In the trench on the inner side, that is towards the interior of the hillfort, two longitudinal beams lay. The inner beam came from the foundations of the chamber construction, while the outer one had originally secured the inclined struts. The space between them was filled with burnt clay from the collapse of the fortification destroyed by fire. On the outer side of the chambers lay a mass of quarried stones from the wall. The chambers of the timber framework were filled with well-rammed earth and the gaps between the beams of the walls were sealed with daub.

The depth of the Slavic ditch was 2.05 m. The ditch had a regular pointed profile and was 5.70 m wide at the upper edge. On its bottom lay a thin deposited layer of clay and small shells. On the basis of these observations it can be said that the fortification on the western side of Hradištia was built along its whole length using the same technique and the same building material. A stone wall (facing) revetted the rampart on the outer side. Only remains of stone, slumped into the ditch, survived of this wall.

blocks.caption: A fine artistic impression of the appearance of the hillfort by our collaborator Anka Kocmaníková
blocks.alt: A fine artistic impression of the appearance of the hillfort by our collaborator Anka Kocmaníková

children.text: A picture of the bend of the fortification in the southern corner of Hradištia was also obtained. This involved the use of a more complex structural element, in which the smooth (fan-like) curve was achieved by changing the shape of the chambers from regular square ones to trapezoidal ones. The stone wall that revetted the rampart then turned in a half-arc and not at a right angle. A bend of the fortification built in this way was more stable and less at risk of being undermined by water run-off than a bend at a right angle.

The rampart was built in the chamber manner with a basic post construction, with wider chambers alternating irregularly with narrower and even very narrow ones. The walls of the rampart chambers were doubled on the outer side (the timbers c. 60 cm apart), but this did not change the basic width of the rampart of 4 m. This doubling of the outer wall was evidently dictated by the palisade, which was set into the crown of the rampart, that is into the space of the doubled outer wall of the chambers, which secured its stability. The interior of the chambers was filled with firmly rammed earth, in which not a single Slavic sherd or object was found. The outer side of the timber-and-earth rampart was revetted by a stone wall, c. 1.50 m thick at the base. The fire that destroyed the hillfort must have been very intense here. In places the timbers of the construction burnt to ash, which was found in fine layers between the clay of the partitions of the chamber construction, fired to a brick-red colour. The building material in the northern part of the hillfort was above all oak (especially pedunculate oak), less often ash. No other woods occurred here. Wattling of withies did not appear on the western and southern sides of Hradištia. In the southern part of the hillfort, good hard timber was saved by not planking the rampart in one stretch of the defences, which had only wattled walls instead. The chamber building type with post construction was indeed retained, but the walls were wattled with branches or withies. The walls were doubled (width c. 60 cm) and dampened earth was rammed between them, which once dried and hardened was a good substitute for planking the walls. When the hillfort was destroyed by fire, these walls were secondarily fired to a brick-red colour. The technique of „ramming" walls (also known as „nabíjanica") survived in Pobedim and in south-western Slovakia right up to the 20th century.

blocks.caption: A few interesting 3D visualisations of the hillfort. Author: NAJ
blocks.alt: A few interesting 3D visualisations of the hillfort. Author: NAJ

children.text: So that a rampart built in this way would be stable and safe, good oak timber was used for the basic post construction, the tie-beams and the inclined struts, more rarely elm, which matches oak in its properties. Willow and other flexible but less good-quality woods served for the wattling of the walls. The palisade was sunk into the doubled walling of the rear side of the chamber, and then came the stone wall that revetted the rampart. The earth for the fill of the chambers was obtained from a shallow, wide ditch on the outer side of the rampart and from the interior enclosure of Hradištia. In many stretches the holes of stouter posts (diameter c. 20 cm) survived, which strengthened the inner wall of the rampart.
The construction of the rampart at Podhradištia

The fortification at Podhradištia had been destroyed long before the excavation began. Along the line where the fortification of the Slavic hillfort ran, the vegetation still has a darker colouring today. A larger quantity of burnt clay was discovered in this part as well, indicating a more extensive collapse of the fortification. Here the rampart consisted of a timber grillage of massive timbers, followed by stone rubble and a shallow ditch. Next, a group of four pits was discovered, forming a regular square in their layout. The arrangement of the post holes is so regular (2.6 × 2.6 m) that it is most probably possible to speak here of the load-bearing construction of a watchtower, which may have had an exit into the marshy hinterland. Judging by the dimensions of the post holes, the load-bearing capacity of the post construction, sunk into regular and deep pits with flat bottoms, was so great that the idea of a two-storey watchtower is entirely realistic. The timber grillage that was identified may be the remains of the lower storey. The width of the chambers of the defences at Podhradištia is 3 m. The fortification around the whole circuit of Podhradištia was of the chamber type, but simpler. It consisted of a timber framework with post construction and wattled walls (width of the chambers c. 3 × 3 m), of a stone wall (width 1.5 m) that revetted the rear side of the rampart, and finally, on the northern and southern sides, of a shallow ditch (depth 0.95 m) a considerable distance away from the rampart. A palisade was sunk into the crown of the timber-and-earth rampart. The inner wall of the rampart was supported by inclined struts, fixed by a longitudinally laid beam secured with pegs. In places the struts were also reinforced with stones. The basic building material was oak. Besides it, other less valuable woods were also used, especially willow branches and withies, which proves that the walls of the chambers were made of wattling, although it cannot be ruled out that here too, in certain stretches — as at Hradištia — they may have been clad with beams or planks. The coating of the walls with daub was used at Podhradištia as well. The same quarried stone was used to build the stone wall as in the construction of the defences at Hradištia. There were probably watchtowers above the western and southern bends. This is suggested by the right-angled bend of the rampart, which created a chamber measuring 3 × 3 m that could easily have carried a single-storey tower superstructure.

The Slavic ditch at Podhradištia was of no great importance from a defensive point of view, because it was shallow and a considerable distance from the rampart (the axis of the ditch is almost 9 m from the axis of the rampart). Besides providing earth for the fill of the rampart, its function may have lain in draining water from the ground in front of the rampart, which had a loose gravelly and sandy subsoil; during floods the water could have threatened the stability of the fortification. And indeed – the excavations suggest that the surroundings of the hillfort were frequently flooded by the Dudváh, or marshy, during the time of its existence. The builders of the fortification of the Slavic hillfort at Pobedim were, however, well acquainted with the water regime of the surrounding terrain. On the one hand they used it as natural protection, and on the other they adapted the fortification system so that the water would not threaten life at the hillfort at times when the water level rose. From this aspect the ditch deserves attention, as it also served to regulate the run-off of water. A sluice gate probably served to regulate the water, especially after Podhradištia was joined to the Hradištia enclosure. The joining of the Podhradištia rampart to the fortification at Hradištia must have been carried out by bridging the ditch.
The choice of the place for construction

The reconstruction of the fortification of the Pobedim hillfort is closely bound up with the reconstruction of its environment. The close tie of the occupation to a particular ecosystem was one of the basic conditions of its prosperity in terms of subsistence (water, soil, woodland, pasture, game, forest fruits), of sources of raw materials (mineral wealth) and of protection. In the choice of the place for the Pobedim hillfort, a role was played not only by the selection of the most suitable place from the point of view of defence, although this aspect was strongly asserted here, but above all by the economic hinterland of the already existing settled oikumene, which in turn depended on the natural conditions. Alongside its shared features, the Pobedim type of fortification differs from similar features in details connected with the local conditions and the local building material.
Consumption of material

In building the fortification of the Slavic hillfort at Pobedim, the building material was obtained from the immediate surroundings within a radius of 5–10 km. The limestone and sandstone from which the outer circuit wall and the covering of the crown of the rampart were built was quarried in the foothills of the Lesser Carpathians and the White Carpathians. The most accessible places for quarrying it are, to this day, in the area around Čachtice and Nové Mesto nad Váhom. In the Slavic period it was probably floated from there down the Dudváh or the Dubová almost as far as the hillfort. Some of the stones may have been taken from the bed of the Váh, which at high water also carried down stones of larger size from distant areas.

The construction of the chamber framework with planking, which at Hradištia runs along a stretch 472 m long, required approximately the following quantity of building material per running metre of the defences: roundwood 2.3 m³ (post construction, planking of the walls, struts, palisade, tie-beams), earth 7 m³ (fill of the chambers, which was obtained from the ditch on the outer side of the fortification, possibly also from the interior enclosure of the hillfort).

children.text: For the wattled construction of Hradištia, 340 m long, approximately the following quantity of building material was used per running metre of the defences: roundwood 0.8 m³ (load-bearing post construction, struts, tie-beams and palisade), wattling of withies and branches of less valuable woods 15 m³, earth 7 m³ (fill of the walling of the chamber construction — the „nabíjanica" — and fill of the chambers), stone for the outer wall and the covering of the crown of the rampart 3.2 m³. On a realistic estimate, the total consumption of building material for building the defences at Hradištia may therefore have been as follows (rm = running metre): roundwood or planks on the stretches of the rampart with planked walls 1,085 m³ (472 rm × 2.3 m³), for the wattled construction 272 m³ (340 rm × 0.8 m³), together 1,357 m³, wattling 5,100 m³ (340 rm × 15 m²), earth 5,684 m³ (812 rm × 7 m³), building stone 2,598 m³ (812 rm × 3.2 m³). Given the length of the defences and the simpler building type, the consumption of building material at Podhradištia was lower.

The building timber was above all oak, sought after for its durability and hardness. It is known that in a suitable environment pedunculate oak lasts as long as 200 years, whereas other woods (apart from elm, which has properties similar to oak) decay and rot relatively quickly. Free access of air speeds this process up. These properties of timber must have been well known to the builders of the hillfort, because they did not use woods of lower building quality at all, or only exceptionally for the struts, the tie-beams and the basic post construction, while they used them freely for the internal division of the rampart. Because the chambers were filled with earth right to the top, the access of air was prevented and the process of decay of the softer and less durable woods was substantially slowed down. The presence of several species of this less valuable building timber in places where watchtowers are assumed documents its use for internal fittings or for other, non-structural purposes. Samples of withies and branches of willow and hazel, preserved in a charred state or as impressions in daub, were found above all in the northern part of the fortification at Hradištia as part of the wattling of the outer walls or as the wattling of the walling of the „nabíjanica" inside the rampart. Their occurrence at Podhradištia is likewise tied to the wattling of the walls of the chamber construction.

It is notable that in certain investigated parts of the hillfort a particular species of wood predominates. It follows from the find situation described that the defences at Hradištia were not built in the same way along their whole length. The basic building type did indeed remain, but various materials were used in building the framework, which called for a different building technique while the same qualities and parameters of the fortification were maintained. The defences at Podhradištia are relatively uniform in character (the chamber type with post construction and with wattled, undoubled walls). The use of different building techniques at one and the same hillfort is unquestionably a reflection of the building of this fortified centre in stages (Hradištia was fortified first and Podhradištia afterwards), but the economic aspect asserted itself here as well. The defences of Podhradištia were already more economical in both time and material than the defences at Hradištia (the rampart is one metre narrower, and the chamber framework with post construction and wattled walls is simple). Building the fortification at Hradištia by two different techniques also arose from the saving of good-quality building material on the side of the hillfort that was protected by the surrounding terrain.

A correctly built timber chamber framework with post construction and wattled walls, filled with firmly rammed earth, performed its function just as well as a log or grillage construction. That is why this structural element was often used, especially at the earlier Slavic hillforts, to a greater or lesser extent in the building of ramparts or of their entrance gateways. The area excavation of the fortification at Hradištia in Pobedim points to a neglect of any regularity in the dimensions of the chambers of the construction. Regular square chambers (4 × 4 m) alternate here with narrower and even very narrow ones, and conversely in places the chambers are more spacious.

The rampart of the Pobedim hillfort, regardless of whether its walls were made by planking or by wattling, had to be secured with tie-beams, above all in the upper part of the chambers and possibly lower down as well. The tie-beams were fastened with pegs (thickness c. 5 cm, length c. 10 cm), which could bear even very great loads. During the excavation of the fortification of the Pobedim hillfort it was established that the chambers of the rampart were deliberately filled with earth on all the investigated stretches, and that this earth was then well rammed. This reduced the angle of friction of the earth and increased the stability of the rampart. The coating of the walls with daub, in which impressions of roundwood, planks or wattling of withies have survived, was likewise intended to prevent the earth from falling through the gaps, which could have caused the construction of the rampart to loosen and gradually collapse.

The surface of the rampart had to be protected against the adverse effect of water erosion. This could be done with a timber decking, but a stone covering of the crown of the rampart could serve the purpose equally well. Besides its protective function and the saving of timber, the stone covering of the crown of the rampart pressed with considerable weight on the upper tie-beams and thereby increased the stability of the rampart. Other technical measures also increased the stability of the rampart. From the interior of the hillfort, inclined oak struts held the rampart at an angle of 60°. Struts placed in this way could hold a rampart 2–3 m high, which is a realistic estimate in the case of Pobedim as well. The spacing of the struts must have been 1–1.50 m. On the outer side, the stability of the rampart was increased by a wall of dry-laid quarried stone, anchored with timber tie-beams. The base of this wall is 1.50 m wide. We assume that the wall narrowed towards the top. A similar width of stone wall was established, for example, at the hillfort in Tlmače and at other Slavic hillforts. The wall lay tight against the body of the rampart, that is, it revetted it, and it certainly reached at least its height; it may have partly protected the lower part of the palisade as well.

For reasons of safety the ditch was a good distance from the rampart itself. Had the ditch been dug closer to the rampart in the soil conditions of the Pobedim area, the looseness of the soil loosened by the action of water would have caused it to slip, and with it the disturbance of the soil base of the rampart.

The average height of the rampart without the palisade superstructure was established as 2.4 m at Hradištia and 2.3 m at Podhradištia. A greater height of the body of the rampart itself cannot be assumed with the building technique used, because the rampart would have collapsed. The height of the rampart was compensated for by setting a palisade into the timber-and-earth body. For the palisade to be properly effective, the timbers had to reach a height that gave adequate cover to a grown man. This means that the palisade projected 2.5–3 m above the crown of the rampart. The stability of such a palisade could be secured only by sinking a fifth of the total length of the timber used (diameter c. 13–21 cm) and then fixing it with well-rammed earth. Mastering the demanding technical requirements of such a structure called for specialists in building fortifications. The palisade around the whole circuit of the hillfort was undoubtedly sunk into the outer wall of the body of the rampart, doubled for this purpose. Otherwise the doubling mentioned cannot be explained. On the inner side, the stability of the palisade was strengthened by struts and by tying with transverse timber. Sound, well-grown timber was used for the palisade, in our case 3–3.5 m long. It can be assumed that the palisade was pointed and that at certain intervals it had viewing slits for the watch. The rampart was reached through the watchtowers or by small steps or ladders.

The total width of the rampart at Hradištia (dimensions of the chambers c. 4 × 4 m), together with the stone wall, is 5.5 m. The anchoring of the inclined struts on the inner side of the hillfort is not counted in this. At Podhradištia the rampart was narrower (chambers measuring c. 3 × 3 m); here the width of the rampart together with the stone wall is 4.5 m. These dimensions correspond to observations at other Slavic hillforts with a timber-and-earth rampart and a stone wall. This type of rampart was widespread above all in the territory of the West Slavs.

An entrance and watchtowers formed part of the fortification of every hillfort. The ground plan of one of them was discovered in that part of the hillfort (Podhradištia) which lay in the immediate vicinity of the natural water reservoir. The existence of watchtowers has to be assumed at the gateways and at the corners of the fortification at Podhradištia and at Hradištia as well. Their placing depended on the position of the hillfort, on the terrain and also on the building technique used. The entrance to the Pobedim hillfort has not yet been established with certainty, even though probable places where the entrance gateways could have stood have been identified. On the north-western side of Podhradištia the load-bearing post construction of a tower was discovered, perhaps with an emergency exit as well. The terrain levelling survey and the data in the old cadastral maps suggest that in the 9th century a natural water reservoir may have existed beyond Podhradištia, into which the emergency exit mentioned may have led. The main entrance to Hradištia was probably on the western side, and a bridge over the deep and regular ditch, which also served as a water regulator, must have formed part of the entrance structure. In case of danger the ditch could always be filled with water from the natural source and thus protect the approach to the hillfort. The way in which the original enclosure of the hillfort was extended makes it possible to assume an entrance gateway into Hradištia in its western part. For strategic reasons it is not likely that each part of the hillfort was entered by a separate gateway. That would be conceivable only if both entrances were protected by a further bailey with a central gateway. Until now, access by land from the eastern or south-eastern side has been preferred. According to new observations, access to the hillfort would not have been from present-day Pobedim but from the direction of the village of Orvište or Ostrov, with the route leading through the north-western part of Podhradištia.
The organisation of construction and defence

Building the hillfort called for good organisation of the individual operations, coordination of the work and the involvement of specialist craftsmen (carpenters, joiners, stonemasons, smiths and so on). Building the whole of the defences at Hradištia in Pobedim (length 812 m) required 49,300 work shifts. The work shifts include the preparation, the transport of material and the actual building of the fortification. With a ten-hour working day this represents the work of 190 people over a period of 260 days; with a larger number of workers the time taken to build the hillfort would have been shorter. Given the simpler technique and the shorter length of the defences, building the defences at Podhradištia required less work. Building the fortification of one part of the hillfort in the course of a calendar year is therefore entirely realistic. It can be said that in the 8th–9th centuries there is a direct dependence between the size of a hillfort and its economic hinterland. The number of workers taking part in building the fortification is roughly the same as the number of defenders needed in times of danger. At Pobedim approximately 260 people were needed to defend the hillfort (one defender for every 5 m). Some of them were inhabitants of the hillfort, but the majority were inhabitants of the surrounding settlements. The economic hinterland of the Pobedim hillfort in the 9th century was formed roughly by the area of the present-day cadastral area of the village, that is c. 900 ha. In this territory, 8 settlements contemporary with the hillfort were discovered during the archaeological excavation.

The fortification of the hillfort called for constant maintenance and, in times of unrest, for defence as well. These works too had to be organised so that not only the inhabitants of the hillfort were involved in them, but also those of the surrounding settlements, who were dependent on the hillfort and its feudal lord. Very interesting data on such an obligation to build, maintain and defend a hillfort is provided by the Anglo-Saxon source The Burhal Hidage of the early 10th century from the Wessex area. It states specifically how much land belonged to the individual hides (a hide being a unit of land) and how many men from each hide were to be at the disposal of the hillfort both in time of peace and in time of danger. For 1 acre of the width of the body of the rampart there was an obligation to supply workers from 16 hides. If a hide was represented by one man, then 4 men fell to 1 yard. This interesting data is a graphic expression of the state of dependence of the inhabitants of the settlements on the hillfort in Wessex and at the same time draws attention to the possibility of analogies in the territory of present-day Slovakia in the 9th–10th centuries.

The Pobedim hillfort is one of the oldest Slavic hillforts in Slovakia. The archaeological material and, most recently, radiocarbon dating as well place it in the period before the rise of Great Moravia (the Blatnica–Mikulčice horizon). The Pobedim hillfort came to a violent end, probably at the time of the parallel advance of Christianisation and of the process of unification. At that time some other hillforts in Slovakia were devastated as well, which can be regarded as the oldest, having come into being before the year 800 or shortly after that date, for example Majcichov, Vyšný Kubín, Spišské Tomášovce and possibly Bojná too.
The present state

Sadly, the village of Pobedim evidently has no interest at present in drawing attention to its exceptionally rich history. The place where the important hillfort originally stood now lies in the middle of a field, and nowhere will you find even a hint of an information panel telling you where the hillfort was. It is a sad picture. Have a look at the photo gallery – the present state of the hillfort as of 7 January 2012.
An update of 10 March 2015. A fine information panel about the hillfort has been installed on the edge of the village, not far from the hillfort. Our thanks and our praise.
